change: Use local row envelopes for shared-axis KKT assembly while retaining the full physical Hessian stencil, original unknown order, exact coefficients and unchanged pivot-capable LU fill. Reuse assembly capacity across compatible factor shapes.
invariants: No change to physical mesh, timestep, tolerances or acceptance certificates.
Every structural Hessian entry stays present even when numerically zero.
Actual constraint supports and nonsymmetric force columns determine local row widths.
Changed public row supports trigger a new envelope before assembly.
Only current row offsets are read when reusing larger assembly buffers.

exactComparison.interpretation: No clear full-scenario speedup: final warm repetition is about 1.15% faster, combined repetitions about 0.18% slower. Earlier paired trials ranged from about 0.6% to 1.6% faster. Timing variation and tail latency exceed this small effect.

scratch.scope: Shared compact numeric buffers only; LU WASM memory capacity remains 2 MiB. This is not a 35% reduction of total application memory.

coverage: Expanded KKT coefficient and solve parity, JS and WASM/prepared and ordinary assembly.
Changing public constraint supports, Hessians and extra force columns.
Arena reuse with changing envelope capacity and stale unused tails.
Full and reduced projection on a captured crossover step that actually exercises projection.
Contact basis, rejected working-set reuse, condensation, modified Newton, native/full-band and LU regression cases.
tests.historicalFixture: The older anatomy projection fixture no longer enters the projection branch in the frozen baseline either. Its physical parity checks remain; explicit projection coverage now also uses the real captured crossover fixture.

limitations: Two 300-step continuations of the captured long-tool crossover, not the complete manual maneuver.
Browser benchmark uses a lightweight preview and excludes full fluoroscopy and app idle catch-up.
No clear full-scenario speedup; this change primarily reduces assembly memory.
60 accepted physics steps per real second remains unachieved.
